questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out the stages a measure passes through.
questions.stem: Using the sequence I watched this season, describe in order the stages a proposed bylaw passed through in the Observers' Assembly, from first reading to enactment.

answer.exemplar: The bylaw went through six stages. First reading introduced the text and printed it for members. Second reading allowed the general debate on the principle of the measure. Third reading was the detailed clause-by-clause examination, when amendments were proposed and voted. Committee stage followed, where a standing committee examined the text and reported back. Report stage returned the measure to the assembly for the final discussion, and the final vote enacted it, after which the instrument was entered in the minute book.

questions.explanation: A measure runs first, second and third readings, committee, report and final vote. Explaining the sequence shows why debate on principle comes before clause examination.
questions.hint: Six stages: three readings, committee, report, vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a rider changes the outcome of a budget.
questions.stem: Combine what I know about appropriations and riders: explain how attaching a policy rider to an appropriation can change the outcome of the budget.

answer.exemplar: An appropriation authorises money to be spent on a stated purpose, and a rider is an unrelated or tangential provision attached to it. Because the assembly votes on the combined text as one instrument, a rider that few members would accept on its own can ride through on the majority that supports the money. The governing risk is that the appropriation becomes hostage to the rider, so the committee chair should move that a rider be split into a separate bill and require that any policy change be justified on its own merits rather than by the strength of the budget vote.

questions.explanation: A rider attaches a policy question to an appropriation so that the money vote carries it. The tempting defence that riders are merely convenient ignores that money and policy are then traded.
questions.hint: The rider travels on the vote for the money.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a guillotine from a plain closure.
questions.stem: Members keep asking what the guillotine actually does to a measure, so set out in your own words how a guillotine differs from an ordinary closure of debate.

answer.exemplar: An ordinary closure of debate simply ends the speeches on a motion, and the assembly then moves on to other business. The guillotine goes further: it closes the debate and at the same time confines the measure to the stage it has already reached, so the remaining clauses are put to the assembly together without further amendment or debate. That is why a guillotine is prized by governments seeking to finish business quickly, and why the opposition resists it: the device protects the principle already accepted but removes the chance to reopen the text clause by clause.

questions.explanation: Closure ends speeches; the guillotine also fixes the measure at its current stage so remaining clauses cannot be amended. A closure that merely defers the item misses that effect.
questions.hint: One cuts speeches, the other cuts amendments.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The legislative calendar and a bill backlog
questions.learningObjective: Propose remedies for a legislative backlog.
questions.stem: Bring together what I have seen of our calendar and our backlog and explain how the assembly could reduce the queue of measures waiting to be heard.

answer.exemplar: The backlog is a scheduling outcome: fixed sittings provide a limited number of debate slots, and any measure that does not reach the floor before the year closes must wait for the next calendar. The first remedy is arithmetic, dividing the measures already in the queue into those with genuine cross-society support and those waiting only for a slot, and using the standing committee to take evidence on the second group. The second remedy is procedural, scheduling a fixed number of measures for each sitting, holding debates to a fixed time, and referring anything that cannot be completed to the committee. The third is to review the calendar's allocation, since a congested calendar wastes debate time on measures that will be superseded.

questions.explanation: A backlog arises when limited sitting time meets more measures than can be heard, so remedies must ration floor time. Leaving the queue untouched assumes demand will fall on its own, which it has not.
questions.hint: Ration floor time rather than add sittings.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: List the devices that control delegated rules.
questions.stem: Describe the ways in which the assembly can bring delegated rules back under its own control, and what each device achieves.

answer.exemplar: Three devices give the assembly control over delegated rules. The first is the report stage: a committee examines the rules the executive has made and reports on them to the floor, which forces the substance into the open and lets members object. The second is the question, which puts a named rule to the secretary and demands an explanation of why it was made and how it will be applied. The third is the requirement to revoke or amend, which demands that a rule cannot stand beyond a defined period unless the assembly renews it. Together these convert open-ended delegation into a supervised stream, because although the assembly may not draft the rules itself, it can examine, question and end them.

questions.explanation: Control comes from examining, questioning and being able to end delegated rules even without drafting them. The assumption that only drafting counts ignores that scrutiny and revocation are control.
questions.hint: Examine, question, and be able to end them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Relate the committee gate to the backlog.
questions.stem: Tie together the committee's role as a gate and the effect of a backlog, and advise the assembly on how the two problems interact.

answer.exemplar: The committee and the backlog are two ends of the same problem. A referral gate holds a measure off the floor, so a committee that sits infrequently converts directly into a queue, and a backlog in turn makes committees the only realistic route for measures that cannot be heard on the floor. The advice is therefore not to treat them separately. The assembly should fix sitting dates at the start of each year and require the committee to report within a fixed number of sitting days of a referral, with an automatic referral back to the floor on expiry. Where a measure cannot be reported in time, the chair should take it directly without requiring the committee's consent, so that the backlog cannot be used as a reason to keep measures waiting.

questions.explanation: A slow gate at committee produces the queue, so fixing the timetable and a reporting deadline addresses both. Treating them as unrelated leaves the committee able to hold bills indefinitely.
questions.hint: A slow gate is where the queue is made.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Orders with the force of law
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish orders, delegated rules and committee decisions.
questions.stem: Set out the differences between a draft order, a delegated rule and a committee resolution, so members stop using the three words interchangeably.

answer.exemplar: A draft order is made by the assembly itself and carries legal force while it stands, ending only when the assembly repeals or amends it. A delegated rule is made by officers under power the assembly has given them, and it depends on that power remaining valid. A committee resolution is a decision of a committee, which may report a recommendation to the assembly but cannot by itself make law unless the assembly later adopts it. The confusion is understandable because all three appear in the minute book, but the consequences differ sharply: a draft order binds at once, a delegated rule can be challenged and revoked, and a committee resolution binds only if the assembly takes it.

questions.explanation: The three differ in maker, in whether they bind at once, and in what ends them. The view that a committee resolution binds because it is minuted ignores that only the assembly can adopt it.
questions.hint: Ask who made it and what ends it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the arguments on unilateral closure.
questions.stem: Weigh the case for and against the chair closing a debate without a vote, and give me a balanced conclusion for the log.

answer.exemplar: The case for the chair acting alone is speed and order. A debate that has repeated its points can be closed on the chair's own initiative, which prevents a determined minority from talking the sitting away and keeps the calendar moving. The case against is that the assembly, not the chair, holds the power to decide how its own time is used, and a unilateral closure can silence a minority at a moment when it matters, particularly on an opposition measure where the speaking order has been arranged to expose weaknesses. The balanced conclusion is that the chair should act alone only where the standing orders clearly permit it and where the debate has demonstrably become repetitive, and should otherwise invite a member to move the closure, which preserves the assembly's authority without wasting more time.

questions.explanation: The chair's power protects order but can silence a minority, so the safeguard is a clear rule plus an invitation to move closure. The absolute of always or never ignores the standing orders.
questions.hint: Weigh both, then read the standing orders.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Trace the full journey of a measure and its failure point.
questions.stem: Explain the full journey of a bylaw through our assembly and say what happens to it if it fails at the third reading.

answer.exemplar: A bylaw is introduced at first reading, when the text is presented and printed so members can see it. Second reading is the debate on the principle of the measure, where the assembly decides whether it wants the policy at all. Third reading is the clause-by-clause examination, the stage at which amendments are proposed, debated and voted, and it is the point of no return for most measures: if the third reading is defeated, the bylaw falls and must be started again from the beginning with a new first reading, and the committee may not revive it later as an amendment to another measure. The measure then goes to a standing committee for evidence and report, returns for the report stage and final discussion, and is enacted on the final vote before being entered in the minute book.

questions.explanation: The journey runs three readings, committee, report and final vote, the third reading being decisive. The belief that a defeated measure can be revived in committee reverses the rule that it starts again.
questions.hint: Third reading is the point of no return.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a rider is and why it is criticised.
questions.stem: Explain what a rider to an appropriation is and why the practice of attaching riders is criticised.

answer.exemplar: An appropriation authorises the government to spend a stated sum on a stated purpose, and a rider is an additional provision attached to the money measure that is not strictly part of that purpose. Because the assembly votes on the combined instrument, a rider can be carried by the majority that wants the money even if very few members would accept the rider on its own. The criticism is that this couples two decisions the assembly should take separately: the amount of money and a policy question become one vote, so the appropriation is effectively held hostage, and a government that needs the money has to buy the rider. The remedy is to require a separate vote on any rider and to forbid its inclusion in the money instrument unless the assembly has first approved it as a separate measure.

questions.explanation: A rider is a provision attached to an appropriation that rides on the money vote, coupling two decisions. The defence that riders are convenient ignores that money and policy can be traded.
questions.hint: Two decisions should not share one vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the guillotine from opposing standpoints.
questions.stem: Assess the guillotine from the standpoint of a member who wants a bill passed, and then from the standpoint of one who wants it improved.

answer.exemplar: For the member who simply wants the measure passed, the guillotine is a gift: it closes debate at a chosen moment and votes the remaining clauses together, so a measure survives even when members disagree about its clauses in detail. Time is saved, the calendar is respected and the outcome is certain, which matters where a governing majority would otherwise lose a clause vote. For the member who wants the measure improved, the same device is a barrier: an amendment that would have attracted support from a wider group of members never reaches the floor, because the clauses are voted as a single block. The balanced conclusion is that the guillotine suits measures that are settled in principle and only need clearance, and misfits measures whose value lies in the detail.

questions.explanation: The guillotine suits a member who wants passage but blocks one who wants improvement, ending debate and voting clauses as a block. The claim that it is simply efficient ignores whose preferences it carries.
questions.hint: Passage and improvement pull opposite ways.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The legislative calendar and a bill backlog
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a backlog affects the quality of debate.
questions.stem: Explain how a backlog of measures can distort the quality of debate as well as its quantity, and what follows for how the assembly should ration time.

answer.exemplar: A backlog changes what gets discussed. When more measures compete for a fixed number of slots than can be heard, the measures that survive are not always the most important but the ones whose sponsors are organised, whose wording is uncomplicated and whose supporters are present that day. Serious measures with wide support but untidy drafting are crowded out, so the quality of deliberation falls even where the quantity of debate has not. The consequence for rationing time is that the assembly cannot simply take measures in the order received; it needs a rule that reserves space for measures with demonstrated cross-society support, and it needs the committee stage to do the tidying work that would otherwise be done in clause debates on the floor.

questions.explanation: Backlogs reward organised sponsors, so quality falls as well as quantity, and rationing must protect well-supported measures. Taking measures in arrival order is not neutral, since it rewards the organised.
questions.hint: Order of arrival is not a neutral rule.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recommend the terms on which power should be delegated.
questions.stem: Bring the arguments together on how much power the assembly should delegate to the secretary, and state what I should write in the log tonight.

answer.exemplar: The case for wider delegation is speed and technical competence. The secretary sees the daily detail of the observatory's work and can settle small matters that would otherwise absorb an evening of members' time, and requiring the assembly to approve every rule would leave the society unable to operate between sittings. The case against wide delegation is that rules made without scrutiny tend to drift away from what the members actually want, and that a body which cannot see the rules cannot hold the officers to them. The compromise is not a single figure of power but a structure: a clear statement of the subject matter delegated, a requirement that the secretary report on each rule made, a defined expiry after which the rule lapses unless the assembly renews it, and a standing committee that keeps a watch list.

questions.explanation: Delegation buys speed, scrutiny protects the assembly's authority, so the answer is delegation with reporting and expiry. The binary of all or nothing ignores that the real question is the terms of delegation.
questions.hint: The terms matter more than the amount.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the balance between committee and floor.
questions.stem: Explain why a committee's power to report a bill back without amendments can matter to the balance between the assembly and the committee.

answer.exemplar: A committee that may report a measure back unaltered has a real gate power, because it can delay a bill and shape the stage at which it returns. If the committee believes the measure should be redrafted, it can return it with recommendations that the assembly usually accepts, and the bill's original momentum, its sponsors and its agreed form are all lost in the process. If the committee must instead report amendments, its influence is limited to proposing changes that the assembly can accept or reject on the floor, and the measure keeps its identity as the sponsors drafted it. The balance therefore turns on what the committee is permitted to return, and a rule that allows unamended reports gives the committee an effective veto on timing and shape.

questions.explanation: A committee allowed to report a bill back unaltered gains delay and influence over form; tabled amendments keep decisions with the floor. The claim that committees merely advise ignores what the report allows.
questions.hint: Ask what the committee may send back.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The legislative calendar and a bill backlog
questions.learningObjective: Identify the main cause of a stalled committee gate.

stimulus.body: Extract from the committee's work table: 38 measures were listed for the year, 12 were reached in committee sessions held in January and February, and the notes record that the remaining 26 were not scheduled because no sessions were fixed for the later months of the year.

questions.stem: From the work table, what is the principal reason the committee's gate held up the calendar?

options.text: The committee lacked the members needed to sit, since the notes mention several vacancies.
options.misconception: invents vacancies that the table does not record

options.text: The committee fixed no sessions after February, so measures were never given a hearing at all.
The measures were too complex for the committee to consider within the year that was available.
options.misconception: assumes complexity rather than scheduling caused the hold-up

options.text: The committee preferred to wait for the assembly to deal with the measures directly on the floor.
options.misconception: ascribes a preference the notes do not support

questions.explanation: The table attributes the hold-up to unscheduled sessions, not to workload or preference. The explanation about complexity misreads an absence of meetings as an inability to deal with the work.
questions.hint: Look for what was not scheduled.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the margin pattern of measures carrying riders.
questions.stem: Appropriation figures for last year: 6 money measures were passed, 11 riders were attached across them, and the two measures carrying the most riders also passed with the narrowest margins. What does this indicate?

options.text: Riders tend to attract opposition, since the measures with riders had the narrowest margins.
options.misconception: reads narrow margins as popular opposition to riders

options.text: Riders make little difference, since six measures passed whatever riders they happened to carry.
options.misconception: treats passage as evidence that riders changed nothing

options.text: Riders may be used to buy support, since the measures carrying the most riders needed the widest agreement.
Narrow margins show the assembly generally dislikes detailed appropriation measures of any kind.
options.misconception: generalises from a few measures to all appropriations

questions.explanation: The measures with the most riders needed the widest agreement, which fits riders used to attract support rather than defeat. The reading that riders attract opposition ignores that a rider can carry votes.
questions.hint: Ask what the riders were there to do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Orders with the force of law
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the benefits and risks of relying on draft orders.
questions.stem: Weigh the advantages and the risks of relying on draft orders to run the society's business, and give me a balanced recommendation for the log.

answer.exemplar: The advantage of draft orders is speed and continuity. The secretary can settle a shutter rule, a loan rule or a site-access rule without waiting for the assembly to meet, and because such an order binds until it is repealed, the rule does not quietly lapse each time attention moves elsewhere. The risk is that an order made in haste by a small group accumulates, and members discover after the fact that they are bound by a long list of decisions they never discussed. The balanced recommendation is to keep the order as the normal instrument, since it is faster than a statute and clearer than a delegated rule, but to attach three safeguards: an entry in the minute book showing the sitting at which it was made, an annual review at which the assembly revokes what it no longer wants, and a register of surviving orders.

questions.explanation: Orders give speed and continuity but accumulate unseen, so the answer is to keep them with a register and an annual review. Abolishing them slows the society for a risk bookkeeping can manage.
questions.hint: Keep the speed, add the visibility.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State whether a rule may be required to be laid before the assembly.
questions.stem: Members wonder whether the assembly can require that a delegated rule be laid before it. What is the correct position?

options.text: Yes, the assembly may require a rule to be laid before it, which obliges the secretary to report on it.
No, laying a rule before the assembly would take away the power the assembly has delegated.
options.misconception: treats reporting as revoking the delegation

options.text: Yes, but only if the rule happens to affect the spending of the society's money.
options.misconception: confines the laying requirement to financial rules

options.text: No, because the assembly may question a rule but can never require it in advance of the making.
options.misconception: assumes questions can never precede the rule

questions.explanation: Laying a rule before the assembly obliges the secretary to report, and does not withdraw the delegation. The view that reporting defeats the power confuses accountability with revocation.
questions.hint: Reporting is not revoking.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of measures ended by a guillotine.
questions.stem: Guillotine arithmetic for the season: 24 measures reached the clause stage, and a guillotine motion was moved on 10 of them. What percentage of the measures that reached the clause stage were ended by a guillotine motion?
questions.explanation: Ten of twenty-four is 41.67 per cent, since 10 divided by 24 is 0.4167. The figures of 10 and 24 give the count and the base rather than the share.
questions.hint: Divide the count by the base, then convert.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply a procedure summary to the stages of a measure.

stimulus.body: Summary of our procedure for the new members: the measure is read a first time, then debated on principle at the second reading, then examined clause by clause at the third reading; a standing committee then reports and the assembly votes finally on the report. The summary adds that a committee may not add clauses to a measure itself.

questions.stem: Using the summary above, which statement about the bill's journey is correct?

options.text: The committee may insert new clauses into the measure before reporting back to the floor.
options.misconception: ignores the summary's explicit limit on committees

options.text: The second reading is where amendments to individual clauses are taken and then voted upon.
options.misconception: puts clause amendment at the principle stage

options.text: The final vote on the report is the stage at which the general debate on principle takes place.
options.misconception: confuses the principle debate with the final vote

options.text: The third reading is the stage at which clause-by-clause amendments are voted upon.

questions.explanation: The summary places clause-by-clause examination at the third reading. The wrong options move clause amendment to the second reading, let committees insert clauses, or move the principle debate.
questions.hint: Third reading is where the clauses are examined.
